summary: Defines a SIP header field returned in responses to REGISTER, so a registrar can tell a user agent a service route to use for outbound requests through the registrar's domain. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When you sign in to a SIP phone system, the registrar that takes your registration can also tell you which proxy to send your outgoing calls through. RFC 3608 defines the header field that carries that information, and the rules for storing it and using it later.

questions: what is the sip service-route header
how does a sip ua learn its service route
what does service-route do in a register response
does service-route apply to incoming sip requests
subtitle: A SIP header that lets a registrar tell a phone which proxies to route its outgoing calls through.

tldr.problem: A SIP user agent that wants outbound services from its home network needs to know which service proxy to use and how to reach it, and that assignment can change dynamically.
tldr.mechanism: The registrar adds a Service-Route header field to its successful REGISTER response. The user agent stores it and may later use it as a preloaded Route header field in its own outgoing initial requests.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3608 is a Proposed Standard. It has since been updated by RFC 5630, and it covers only requests that the user agent originates, not ones sent to it.

today: RFC 3608 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2003 and has been updated by RFC 5630. It has not been obsoleted. The text itself says nothing about deployments.

sections.title: Background
sections.content:
The Third Generation Partnership Project established a requirement for discovering home proxies during SIP registration and published it in a separate document. The 3GPP network dynamically assigns a home service proxy to each address-of-record. This assignment may occur in conjunction with a REGISTER operation, or out-of-band as needed to support call services when the address-of-record has no registrations. The home service proxy may provide both inbound, UA terminated, and outbound, UA originated, services.

In the inbound case, the Request-URI of incoming SIP requests matches the address-of-record of a user associated with the home service proxy, and the home service proxy then, in most cases, forwards the request to the registered contact address for that address-of-record.

Outbound, UA originated, session cases raise another issue: how does the UA know which service proxy to use and how to get there? Several mechanisms were proposed in list discussions.

Configuration data in the UA raises questions of configuration management and updating, especially if proxy assignment is very dynamic, such as in load-balancing scenarios. Use of some other protocol, such as HTTP, to get configuration data from a configuration server in the home network is functional but requires additional protocol engines, firewall complexity, operations overhead and significant additional over-the-air traffic. Use of lookup tables in the home network, as may be done for inbound requests in some 3G networks, has a relatively high overhead in terms of database operations. Returning a 302 response indicating the service proxy as a new contact shares the database operation of the previous alternative, but explicitly allows the 302 response to be cached, potentially reducing the frequency and number of database operations.

Performing an operation equivalent to record-routing in a REGISTER transaction between the UA and the associated registrar, then storing that route in the UA and reusing it as a service route on future requests originating from the UA, is efficient but constrains the service route for proxy operations to be congruent with the route taken by the REGISTER message. Finally, returning service route information as the value of a header field in the REGISTER response is similar to the previous alternative, but grants the ability for the registrar to selectively apply knowledge about the topology of the home network in constructing the service route. This document defines that final alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone that has signed in to its home network needs to know which proxy to use for its outgoing calls, and that assignment can change at any time. The document lists six ways this could be solved and explains why the last one is the one it standardises: telling the phone in the reply to its registration.

sections.title: Discussion of Mechanism
sections.content:
UAs may include a Route header field in an initial request to force that request to visit and potentially be serviced by one or more proxies. Using such a route, called a service route or preloaded route, allows a UA to request services from a specific home proxy or network of proxies. The open question is how a UA may discover what service route to use.

This document defines a header field called Service-Route which can contain a route vector that, if used as described, will direct requests through a specific sequence of proxies. A registrar may use a Service-Route header field to inform a UA of a service route that, if used by the UA, will provide services from a proxy or set of proxies associated with that registrar. The Service-Route header field may be included by a registrar in the response to a REGISTER request, so a registering UA learns of a service route that may be used to request services from the system it just registered with.

The routing established by the Service-Route mechanism applies only to requests originating in the user agent. That is, it applies only to UA originated requests, and not to requests terminated by that UA.

Simply put, the registrar generates a service route for the registering UA and returns it in the response to each successful REGISTER request. This service route has the form of a Route header field that the registering UA may use to send requests through the service proxy selected by the registrar. The UA would use this route by inserting it as a preloaded Route header field in requests originated by the UA and intended for routing through the service proxy. The mechanism by which the registrar constructs the header field value is specific to the local implementation and outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The new header field carries a list of proxies, in order, that the phone should send its outgoing calls through. It only applies to calls the phone starts, not to calls coming in to it.

sections.title: Applicability Statement
sections.content:
The Service-Route mechanism is applicable when the UA registers with a registrar; when the registrar has knowledge of a service proxy that should be used by the UA when requesting services from the domain of the registrar, which may be a result of dynamic assignment or some other mechanism outside the scope of this document; when the registrar or registrars have sufficient knowledge of the network topology, policy and situation such that a reasonable service route can be constructed; when the service route constructed by the registrar is the same for all contacts associated with a single address-of-record, since this mechanism does not provide for contact-specific service routes; and when other mechanisms for proposing a service route to the UA are not available or are inappropriate for use within the specific environment.

Other methods may also be available by which a UA may be informed of a service route, and such alternative methods are outside the scope of this document, as is the discussion of why one might wish to assign a service route during registration or when it might be appropriate to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism is for the case where the registrar already knows which proxy the phone should use and can build a sensible route. It gives one route per address, not a different route for each device, and it does not replace other ways of telling a phone about a proxy.

sections.title: Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax for the Service-Route header field is:

Service-Route = "Service-Route" HCOLON sr-value *( COMMA sr-value)

sr-value = name-addr *( SEMI rr-param )

The Service-Route header field values MUST conform to the syntax of a Route element as defined in the SIP specification. As suggested there, such values MUST include the loose-routing indicator parameter ;lr for full compliance.

The document also adds Service-Route to the table of allowable usage of header fields in the SIP specification. The new entry places Service-Route in 2xx responses, marks it as allowed in a proxy column, and marks it as optional in a REGISTER column, with dashes for the other request types.
sections.plainLanguage: The header field holds a comma-separated list of addresses, each with the ;lr parameter that tells a proxy to keep routing the request onwards rather than stopping there.

sections.title: Usage
sections.content:
At the UA, the registration is performed as usual and the REGISTER response may contain a Service-Route header field. If so, the UA MAY store the value in association with the address-of-record for which the REGISTER transaction registered a contact. A UA that supports multiple addresses-of-record may be able to store multiple service routes, one per address-of-record. If the UA refreshes the registration, the stored value is updated according to the Service-Route header field of the latest 200 class response. If there is no Service-Route header field in the response, the UA clears any service route previously stored for that address-of-record. If the re-registration request is refused, or if an existing registration expires and the UA chooses not to re-register, the UA SHOULD discard any stored service route for that address-of-record.

The UA MAY choose to exercise a service route for future requests associated with a given address-of-record. If so, it uses the content of the Service-Route header field as a preloaded Route header field in outgoing initial requests. The UA MUST preserve the order, in case there is more than one Service-Route header field or header field value. The specifics of how the service route set integrates with any locally required default route and local policy are implementation dependent; some devices will use locally-configured explicit loose routing to reach a next-hop proxy, and others will use a default outbound-proxy routing rule. In general, the service route set is appended to any locally configured route needed to egress the access proxy chain.

At the proxy, the Service-Route header field is generally treated like any other unknown header field by intermediate proxies, which simply forward it on towards the destination. Proxies should not assume that they will be traversed by future requests in a dialog simply because they appear in the Service-Route header field.

There is a question of whether proxies processing a REGISTER response may add themselves to the route set in the Service-Route header field. This would enable dynamic construction of service routes, but it has two significant problems. The first is transparency, as seen by the registrar: intermediate proxies could add themselves without the knowledge or consent of the registrar. The second is interaction with end-to-end security. If the registrar uses S/MIME techniques to protect the REGISTER response, such additions would be visible to the UA as man in the middle alterations in the response. Consequently, intermediate proxies SHOULD NOT alter the value of Service-Route in REGISTER responses, and if they do, the UA MUST NOT be required to accept the alteration.

Proxies that are dual homed, meaning connected to two or more different networks such that requests are received on one interface and proxied out through another, complicate matters. Instead of following the standard procedure, proxies used with Service-Route that are inserting Record-Route or Path header field values SHOULD record not one but two route values when processing the request. The first value recorded indicates the receiving interface, and the second indicates the sending interface. When processing the response, no modification of the recorded route is required. This provides for fully invertible routes that can be effectively used in the construction of service routes.

At the registrar, when a registrar receives a successful REGISTER request, it MAY choose to return one or more Service-Route header fields in the 200 class response. Whether to include them and what values to insert are matters of local policy. Having inserted them, the registrar returns the 200 class response to the UA in accordance with standard procedures. A REGISTER operation performing a Fetching Bindings, that is, no Contact header field present in the request, SHOULD return the same value of Service-Route as returned in the corresponding previous REGISTER response for the address-of-record in question. A Fetching Bindings operation could be used by the UA to recover a lost value of Service-Route, or the UA could just re-REGISTER.

Certain network topologies MAY require a specific proxy, such as a firewall proxy, to be traversed before the home service proxy. A registrar with specific knowledge of the network topology MAY therefore return more than one Service-Route header field or element in the 200 class response; the order is specified as top-down, meaning the topmost Service-Route entry will be visited first. In general, the Service-Route header field contains references to elements strictly within the administrative domain of the registrar and home service proxy. For example, consider a case where a user leaves the home network and roams into a visited network. The registrar cannot be assumed to have knowledge of the topology of the visited network, so the Service-Route it returns contains elements only within the home network.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone stores the route it was given, and refreshes or drops it as the registration changes. When it makes a call it can put the stored route into the Route header. Proxies pass the header along untouched, because a proxy that quietly added itself would break the registrar's view and would show up as a man in the middle alteration to the phone.

sections.title: Examples of Usage
sections.content:
The example is set in a home network containing a routing proxy P2, a registrar R, a home service proxy HSP, and a database used by both R and HSP. P2 is the edge of the home network from a SIP perspective. UA1 is an external user agent behind proxy P1, and UA2 is another user agent on the Internet that does not use a default outbound proxy.

In the REGISTER transaction, UA1 registers to HOME.EXAMPLE.COM using registrar R. R returns a Service-Route indicating that UA1 may use the home service proxy HSP.HOME.EXAMPLE.COM to receive outbound services from HOME.EXAMPLE.COM. The registrar is statically configured to reference HSP as a service route, and it also knows that P2 is used as the provider edge proxy, so it returns:

Service-Route: <sip:P2.HOME.EXAMPLE.COM;lr>,
               <sip:HSP.HOME.EXAMPLE.COM;lr>

The response travels back through P2 and P1 to UA1, which stores the service route for its address-of-record.

In the INVITE transaction, UA1 places a call to UA2 using the outbound services of HOME.EXAMPLE.COM, which provides a logging service that records the call. UA1 inserts the stored route as a Route header field, with the same two entries, and P1 forwards the request while adding itself to the Record-Route. P2 removes itself from the Route, adds itself to the Record-Route and forwards the request to HSP, which was selected using a DNS lookup for HSP within HOME.EXAMPLE.COM. HSP executes the service, writing a record to the log book, then looks up the address-of-record for UA2 and discovers that the current contact is at host UAADDR2.HOME.EXAMPLE.COM, which becomes the Request-URI of the next-hop INVITE. HSP removes itself from the Route and forwards the request onward, which propagates towards UA2 as usual.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example shows a phone registering and receiving a two-entry route, then making a call that travels through both proxies so that the home proxy can record the call before the request continues.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
It is possible for proxies between the UA and the registrar during the REGISTER transaction to modify the value of Service-Route returned by the registrar, or to insert a Service-Route even when one was not returned. The consequence of such an attack is that future requests made by the UA using the service route might be diverted to or through a node other than would normally be visited. It is also possible for proxies on the INVITE path to execute many different attacks. It is therefore desirable to apply transitive mutual authentication using sips: or other available mechanisms in order to prevent such attacks.

The sips: URI defines a mechanism by which a UA may request transport-level message integrity and mutual authentication. Since there is no requirement for proxies to modify messages, S/MIME signed bodies may be used to provide end-to-end protection for the returned value.

Systems using Service-Route SHOULD provide hop-by-hop message integrity and mutual authentication. UAs SHOULD request this support by using a sips: URI. Registrars returning a Service-Route MUST implement end-to-end protection using S/MIME and SHOULD use S/MIME to protect all such responses. UAs receiving Service-Route SHOULD authenticate attached S/MIME bodies if present.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy on the way back from the registrar could rewrite the route and send the phone's future calls somewhere else. To stop that, the registrar should sign the response it sends back, and the phone should check the signature and use a secure URI scheme.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines the SIP extension header field Service-Route, which has been included in the registry of SIP header fields defined in the SIP specification. The change process for SIP mandates that general SIP extension header fields be defined by a standards-track RFC, and this document provides the required definition.

The registration gives the RFC number as RFC 3608, the header field name as Service-Route, and the compact form as none.
sections.plainLanguage: The header field has been added to IANA's list of SIP header fields, with no short form.
